title: Weather and Seasons
subtitle: Weather, seasons and plans in Dunmore

parts.title: Weather warnings and changes of plan
parts.instructions: For each notice, choose what it means.
notices: DUNMORE COUNCIL: Strong winds are expected tonight. Please bring in bins, garden chairs and anything else that could blow away.
FERRY NOTICE: Because of fog on the bay, the 10.15 ferry will leave about an hour late. Passengers can wait in the ticket hall, where hot drinks are half price.
YOSSI: Saturday’s match is off because the pitch is flooded. Coach says we’ll play next week instead. Can you tell the others? I’ve got no signal.
TO ALL RESIDENTS: The heating in Block C will be switched on from Monday because of the cold weather. If your radiators are still cold on Tuesday, please call the office.
FROST ALERT AT THE GARDEN CENTRE: Temperatures will fall below zero this week. Cover young plants with warm cloth (£2 a roll) or bring pots indoors overnight.

questions.prompt: What are residents asked to do?
questions.explanation: The council asks people to bring in bins, chairs and anything that could blow away in the wind.

questions.prompt: What does the notice say?
options: The ferry has been cancelled until noon.
The ferry will be later than planned.
questions.explanation: The 10.15 ferry will leave about an hour late because of the fog.

questions.prompt: What does Yossi ask his friend to do?
options: Bring his spare kit to the pitch on Thursday.
Tell the rest of the team about the match.
Look at the forecast for the next few days.
questions.explanation: The match is off, and Yossi asks his friend to let the others know.

questions.prompt: When should residents call the office?
options: If the heating comes on earlier than planned.
As soon as it starts to get really cold outside.
If the radiators are still cold on Tuesday.
questions.explanation: The heating starts on Monday; if the radiators are still cold on Tuesday, residents should call.

questions.prompt: What does the garden centre recommend?
questions.explanation: It says to cover young plants with warm cloth or bring pots indoors overnight, because of the frost.

parts.title: Seasonal events in Dunmore
parts.instructions: Read what each person is looking for. Match each person to the best event. There are three extra events.

people.text: Javier wants a cheap outdoor activity for his two young daughters on a windy Sunday afternoon.
Tabitha enjoys taking photographs of trees. She would like to join a group walk when the leaves change colour.
Karol wants to buy Christmas presents made by local people, and he would like to warm up with hot food at the same time.
Penelope has just moved to a house with a bare garden and would like to learn how to grow vegetables.
Caleb wants to do something useful for the environment with his friends one morning. He does not own any tools.

texts.title: Beach clean-up
texts.text: Meet at the harbour car park on Saturday at 9 a.m. We provide gloves and bags. Come for an hour or stay all morning.

texts.title: Christmas craft evening
texts.text: Make your own presents from wood and paper in the village hall. Hot soup is served. Friday at 6 p.m.

texts.title: Spring planting day
texts.text: Learn how to sow seeds and look after young vegetables in the community garden. All beginners are welcome and seeds are free.

texts.title: Allotment visit
texts.text: Walk round the allotments and look at fruit and vegetables growing. No lessons are given, and visitors may not touch the plants.

texts.title: Ice-skating night
texts.text: Skate under the lights at the temporary rink in the town square. Skates can be hired for £4. Open every evening until 9 p.m.

texts.title: Autumn woodland walk
texts.text: A gentle four-mile walk through Dunmore Woods with a ranger, when the leaves are at their most colourful. Stop for photos along the way. Groups meet at the gate at 10 a.m.

texts.title: Winter market
texts.text: More than fifty stalls selling handmade gifts, candles and toys from local makers. Warm up with soup, hot chocolate or roasted chestnuts.

texts.title: Kite day
texts.text: Bring a kite or make one with us on the hill on Sunday from 2 to 4 p.m. It’s free, and the best days are windy ones. Families welcome.

questions.prompt: Javier
questions.explanation: Javier wants a cheap outdoor activity for his daughters on a windy Sunday; Kite day is free, on a Sunday afternoon, and is best on windy days.

questions.prompt: Tabitha
questions.explanation: Tabitha likes photographing trees and wants a group walk in autumn; the woodland walk is led by a ranger when the leaves are colourful, with stops for photos.

questions.prompt: Karol
questions.explanation: Karol wants handmade presents and hot food; the winter market sells handmade gifts and has soup and hot chocolate.

questions.prompt: Penelope
questions.explanation: Penelope wants to learn to grow vegetables; the spring planting day teaches beginners how to sow seeds and look after vegetables.

questions.prompt: Caleb
questions.explanation: Caleb wants to help the environment and has no tools; the beach clean-up provides gloves and bags.

parts.title: A very hot summer in the city
parts.instructions: Read the text and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
When I moved to the city last June, everyone told me the summers there were mild. They were wrong. By the second week, the temperature had reached thirty-five degrees and stayed there. My flat is on the top floor, and by the afternoon it felt like an oven. I could not sleep, and my small fan only moved the hot air around.

An elderly neighbour gave me some advice. He told me to keep the curtains and windows closed during the day and to open everything at night, when it cools down. It sounds obvious, but it made a real difference. I also started going to the public library after work, because it was cool inside, and I got a lot of reading done.

The hottest day was a Saturday in July. I could not stand my flat any longer, so I went down to the fountain in the main square. Children were splashing about, and even the adults had taken off their shoes. I joined them, and for the first time I talked to some people who lived in my building.

Now autumn has arrived, and I am almost sorry. I still complain about the heat when I remember it, but that summer gave me friends I would never have met otherwise.

questions.prompt: What had the writer been told about the city’s summers?
options: They were longer than in other cities.
They were often wet and windy.
They were colder than in other cities.
They did not get very hot at all.
questions.explanation: Everyone said the summers there were mild, which means not very hot.

questions.prompt: What does the writer say about her fan?
options: It was too noisy to sleep with at night.
It did not really make her cooler.
It stopped working in the first week.
It stopped working in the heat of July.
questions.explanation: The fan only moved the hot air around, so it did not cool the room.

questions.prompt: What did her neighbour advise her to do?
options: Spend the hottest hours of the day in the library.
Buy an air conditioner for the bedroom.
Close the windows by day and open them at night.
Sleep on the floor at night.
questions.explanation: He told her to keep the curtains and windows closed during the day and to open everything at night.

questions.prompt: What happened at the fountain?
options: She met some of the people in her building.
She took photos of the children playing there.
She talked to a police officer.
She was asked to put her shoes back on.
questions.explanation: She talked to people from her building for the first time.

questions.prompt: How does the writer feel about the summer now?
options: Relieved that the hot weather is over.
Keen to move to a cooler city.
Keen to move to a different flat.
A little sad that it has finished.
questions.explanation: She is “almost sorry” that autumn has arrived because the summer gave her new friends.

parts.title: A village after the floods
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There are three extra sentences.
parts.passage:
Last winter, heavy rain fell on Dunmore for nearly two weeks. The river rose slowly at first, and then very quickly one night in January. [1] By morning, the water was a metre deep in the main street.

Most families had time to leave, and the village hall became a shelter for fifty people. [2] Neighbours who had hardly spoken before were suddenly sharing blankets and soup. Local farmers arrived with tractors to move furniture to higher ground.

When the water finally went down, the real work began. [3] Volunteers from nearby towns came to help shovel mud out of the houses, and the bakery, which had lost all its flour, reopened after ten days.

Six months later, the village looks almost normal. [4] The council has also promised a higher wall beside the river, which should be finished next year. [5] “We were lucky to have each other,” said one shopkeeper.
sentences: Many residents say the flood has made the community stronger.
Cleaning up took far longer than anyone had expected.
Heavy rain was forecast again for the following weekend.
Most of the damaged houses have been repaired, and families are living in them again.
The river is the longest in the county.
Nobody in the village had expected the water to rise so fast.
The mayor visited the village the week after.
It was crowded and noisy, but people stayed remarkably cheerful.

gaps.explanation: “Nobody had expected the water to rise so fast” follows “very quickly one night”, and “By morning” continues the story.
“It” refers to the village hall; the cheerful mood leads to the next sentence about neighbours sharing blankets and soup.
“Cleaning up took far longer than anyone had expected” follows “the real work began” and leads to the volunteers shovelling mud.
Repaired houses show the village looks “almost normal”, and “also” in the next sentence adds another good thing, the higher wall.
The comment that the flood made the community stronger leads to the shopkeeper’s quote. Sentence C is about future rain and fits no gap.

parts.title: Packing for a rainy holiday
parts.instructions: Choose the correct word for each gap.
parts.passage: If you are going on holiday to a country where it rains a lot, it is important to [1] carefully. A good raincoat is much better than an umbrella, because strong wind can [2] an umbrella inside out in seconds. You should also take shoes that keep your feet [3] when you walk through puddles. Pack spare socks in a plastic bag, [4] wet socks can spoil a day out. A small waterproof bag will protect your phone and any [5] papers. Finally, remember that rain does not have to ruin a trip, as long as you are [6].

questions.prompt: Gap 1
questions.explanation: “Pack carefully” is the natural expression for getting your luggage ready.

questions.prompt: Gap 2
questions.explanation: Wind can blow an umbrella inside out; this is the usual collocation.

questions.prompt: Gap 3
questions.explanation: Shoes for puddles should keep your feet dry.

questions.prompt: Gap 4
questions.explanation: “Because” gives the reason for packing spare socks: wet socks can spoil a day.

questions.prompt: Gap 5
questions.explanation: You want to protect “important papers” such as tickets and passports.

questions.prompt: Gap 6
questions.explanation: “As long as you are prepared” means ready for the weather.

parts.title: A postcard from a snowy holiday
parts.instructions: Write one word in each gap.
parts.passage:
Dear Rhiannon,
Greetings from the mountains! It has been snowing [1] Monday, and everything looks like a Christmas card. We have been here [2] five days now. This morning we learnt to ski, [3] I fell over a lot. The hotel is warm, so we sit [4] the fire in the evenings and drink hot chocolate. Tomorrow, if the weather is better [5] today, we are going to take the cable car to the top. I wish you [6] here with us!
Love,
Dewi

gaps.explanation: The snow began on Monday and continues now, so we use “since” with the present perfect continuous.
“For” goes with a period of time: “for five days”.
“But” contrasts learning to ski with falling over a lot.
“By the fire” means next to it.
“I wish you were here” is the fixed pattern for a wish about the present.

parts.title: Short conversations about the weather
parts.instructions: Listen to seven short conversations. Choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: sunil
turns.text: Indira, are we still having the barbecue on Saturday? The forecast looks cloudy.

turns.speaker: indira
turns.text: I checked this morning. Saturday should be dry, but a bit windy. We can put the grill at the back of the house, it’s sheltered there.

turns.speaker: sunil
turns.text: Hmm. What about Sunday afternoon instead? I’m free all day.

turns.speaker: indira
turns.text: The forecast says heavy rain from midday on Sunday. And next weekend I’m away at my sister’s, so that’s no good either.

turns.speaker: sunil
turns.text: Okay, so the first plan was the right one. I’ll buy the sausages tonight.

turns.speaker: indira
turns.text: And don’t forget to ask the neighbours. They always bring a lot of food.

question.prompt: When will they have the barbecue?
question.explanation: Sunday afternoon will be rainy and Indira is away next weekend, so they keep their first plan for Saturday.

turns.speaker: tamar
turns.text: Naveen, it’s pouring. How will you get home?

turns.speaker: naveen
turns.text: I wore my raincoat to work yesterday and left it at my parents’ house. Typical!

turns.speaker: tamar
turns.text: You can borrow mine. It’s in the cupboard.

turns.speaker: naveen
turns.text: It’s bright pink and far too small, but thanks. I have a hat in my bag, but it’s useless, my neck always gets wet.

turns.speaker: tamar
turns.text: So what will you do?

turns.speaker: naveen
turns.text: My dad is coming to pick up a parcel in ten minutes. He always has two umbrellas in his car, so I’ll take one of them.

turns.speaker: tamar
turns.text: Great idea. Stay dry!

question.prompt: What will Naveen use to keep dry?
options: A hat that keeps off the rain
question.explanation: Tamar’s raincoat is too small and the hat is useless, but his father always has two umbrellas in his car and is coming soon.

turns.speaker: ciara
turns.text: Hi Nolan, it’s Ciara. About tomorrow. The radio says there will be thick snow tonight, so the buses might not run, and I won’t take the bus if it stops in the middle of the road. I thought about driving slowly, but our road is steep and I don’t have winter tyres, so I’d rather not risk it. The school is only twenty-five minutes away on foot, and I have good boots, so I’ll just walk. I’ll leave early, at seven. I nearly asked you for a lift, but you start work on the other side of town. Please tell the head teacher if I’m late. Thanks. Bye!

question.prompt: How will the woman get to school?
question.explanation: The buses may not run and she does not want to drive on the steep road in the snow, so she will go on foot.

turns.speaker: tara
turns.text: Kane, we’re nearly out of sun cream, and the forecast for the beach is thirty degrees.

turns.speaker: kane
turns.text: There’s an old bottle in the bathroom. Use that.

turns.speaker: tara
turns.text: It’s from two summers ago, it doesn’t work any more. I’d ask you to buy some, but you’re at work until six and the shops close at half past five.

turns.speaker: kane
turns.text: True. So what are you going to do?

turns.speaker: tara
turns.text: There’s a pharmacy at the station that’s open late. I’ll buy some on my way there.

turns.speaker: kane
turns.text: Good plan. Get factor fifty, please. The last one burned me.

question.explanation: The old bottle is no good and Kane finishes work after the shops close, so Tara will buy it herself at the pharmacy on the way to the station.

turns.speaker: alana
turns.text: Oh no, it’s starting to rain on our picnic.

turns.speaker: joaquin
turns.text: Shall we go home and finish it in the kitchen?

turns.speaker: alana
turns.text: It’s an hour on the bus, and the sandwiches would get soggy. Look, there are some trees by the lake.

turns.speaker: joaquin
turns.text: We could eat our lunch inside the car instead, but it’s parked a long way away, and the heater is broken.

turns.speaker: alana
turns.text: The trees will keep us dry, and just behind them there’s an old shelter with a roof. Let’s move the blanket there.

turns.speaker: joaquin
turns.text: Good idea. Grab the bags.

question.prompt: What do they decide to do?
options: Move to a more sheltered place
Go home and finish the picnic there
Eat their lunch inside the car instead
question.explanation: Going home takes an hour and the car is far away, so they decide to go to the old shelter behind the trees.

turns.speaker: emil
turns.text: Noura, it’s Emil. You asked about the torch for tonight’s camping trip. I looked in the kitchen drawer where we usually keep it, but there are only batteries there. I thought it might be in the car, so I checked, and it wasn’t. Then I remembered that I used it last week when the lights went out. I put it on the small table near the front door, next to the umbrella. Yes, it’s in the hall, with the keys. I’ll bring it with me when I leave. See you at six.

question.explanation: It is not in the kitchen drawer or the car; Emil left it on the table near the front door, with the keys.

turns.speaker: natalie
turns.text: Brr, it’s freezing! My hands are like ice.

turns.speaker: karthik
turns.text: Here, take my scarf.

turns.speaker: natalie
turns.text: It’s too thin, and you’ll need it.

turns.speaker: karthik
turns.text: My winter coat, then? I’m warm, so I don’t need it.

turns.speaker: natalie
turns.text: Your coat is enormous on me. Don’t you have something for my hands?

turns.speaker: karthik
turns.text: Oh, of course. I have a pair in my pocket. Here you are.

turns.speaker: natalie
turns.text: Thanks, you’re a hero. These gloves are lovely and warm already. Now I can finally enjoy this walk by the river with you.

turns.speaker: karthik
turns.text: You’re welcome. We can go home when you want.

question.prompt: What does Natalie borrow from Karthik?
question.explanation: The scarf is too thin and the coat is too big, but she wants something for her hands, so she takes what he has in his pocket, his gloves.

parts.title: Everyday weather situations
parts.instructions: Listen to six short conversations and choose the best answer.

turns.speaker: riley
turns.text: It’s so hot in my flat. I can’t sleep or work.

turns.speaker: quinn
turns.text: Have you tried a fan?

turns.speaker: riley
turns.text: Maybe I should buy one. Or I could work at home in the evenings, when it’s cooler.

turns.speaker: quinn
turns.text: A fan only moves hot air, so don’t waste your money. And you’d still sleep badly. Why not go to the coast for a few days? It’s much cooler there.

turns.speaker: riley
turns.text: But I have so much work.

turns.speaker: quinn
turns.text: You can take your laptop. The sea air will do you good.

turns.speaker: riley
turns.text: You know, that’s actually a great idea.

options: Working from home in the evening
Buying a fan for his flat

turns.speaker: ramon
turns.text: Are we still having the party in the garden on Saturday?

turns.speaker: sorcha
turns.text: I’m not sure. The forecast says sun, but last time it said that, and it poured.

turns.speaker: ramon
turns.text: The garden is big enough for everyone, I counted.

turns.speaker: sorcha
turns.text: Yes, size isn’t the problem, and the food is cheap, I’ve done the shopping. But what if the forecast is wrong again?

turns.speaker: ramon
turns.text: We could borrow a tent from my uncle, just in case.

turns.speaker: sorcha
turns.text: Okay, that makes me feel better.

options: The garden is too small for everyone.
The food will cost too much money.

turns.speaker: eleanor
turns.text: Tomasz, you’re forty minutes late! What happened?

turns.speaker: tomasz
turns.text: Sorry. The fog was terrible on the motorway. I could hardly see ten metres, so I had to drive slowly, at thirty miles an hour, for nearly an hour.

turns.text: Did the car break down? You said last week it was making a noise.

turns.speaker: tomasz

turns.speaker: eleanor
turns.text: Well, I’m glad you’re safe. Come in and have some tea.

turns.speaker: tomasz

question.explanation: The car is fine and he did not get lost; the thick fog made him drive very slowly.

turns.speaker: tamar
turns.text: Joaquin, is tomorrow’s school trip happening?

turns.speaker: joaquin
turns.text: I heard the school was going to cancel it, but the head teacher said no, not yet. And it isn’t moved to next week either. They’ll decide tomorrow at seven, after checking the forecast, so everything depends on the weather.

turns.speaker: tamar
turns.text: So if it rains...

turns.speaker: joaquin
turns.text: If there’s heavy rain, we stay at school. If it’s only cloudy, we go.

turns.speaker: tamar
turns.text: I’ll pack my bag tonight anyway.

turns.speaker: joaquin
turns.text: Me too. And I’m bringing a raincoat, just in case.

turns.speaker: tamar

question.prompt: What does Joaquin say about tomorrow's trip?
options: It has already been cancelled by the school.
It has been moved to next week.
question.explanation: It is not cancelled and not moved; the teachers will decide in the morning after seeing the forecast, so it depends on the weather.

turns.speaker: noura
turns.text: How was the festival, Kane? I heard it rained all weekend.

turns.speaker: kane
turns.text: Don’t remind me. I was soaked to my socks. But it was great fun.

turns.speaker: noura
turns.text: Were the bands good?

turns.speaker: kane
turns.text: Some were average, but the main band was fantastic, and everyone was singing in the mud.

turns.speaker: noura
turns.text: Do you regret going?

turns.speaker: kane
turns.text: Not at all. I’d go again tomorrow. I’d just wear better boots, that’s all. Next year you should come with me.

turns.speaker: noura
turns.text: Maybe, if they promise some sun.

question.prompt: How did Kane feel about the festival?
options: He enjoyed it despite the rain.
He was disappointed by the bands.
He wished he had stayed at home.
question.explanation: He was wet, but he says it was great fun, the main band was fantastic and he does not regret going.

turns.speaker: nolan
turns.text: My jacket is useless. My shirt got wet on the way here.

turns.speaker: alana
turns.text: I was in town yesterday, and Greenfield’s has a sale. Rain jackets are half price this week.

turns.speaker: nolan
turns.text: I need boots too.

turns.speaker: alana
turns.text: They’re not in the sale. There’s another shop on Mill Road that mends coats, but the zip on yours isn’t broken, it’s just old.

turns.speaker: nolan
turns.text: Half price sounds good. How much is it?

turns.speaker: alana
turns.text: About twenty pounds. I’ll go on Friday.

turns.speaker: nolan
turns.text: I’ll go on Friday too.

turns.speaker: alana
turns.text: Go before Saturday, the sale ends then.

question.prompt: What does Alana tell Nolan about?
options: A cheaper place to buy boots
question.explanation: Boots are not in the sale and a repair shop would not help; she tells him about a half-price sale on rain jackets.

parts.title: A weather presenter talks about April
parts.instructions: Listen to the talk and complete each note. Write one or two words, a number, a date or a time.

turns.speaker: speaker-1
turns.text: Hello, everyone. I’m Tabitha, and every morning I present the weather on Dunmore Radio. Today I’m going to tell you what to expect in April, and how to enjoy it. The first thing to know is that April weather changes very quickly. You can have sunshine, a short shower and even a little hail in one afternoon, so don’t trust the sky at breakfast. Now some tips. If you want to go for a walk, the best time is the morning. The afternoons are often wetter, because clouds build up after lunch, and the evenings are cold. I walk by the river at eight, before most people are up. If you plan a trip to the coast, remember that it’s quite windy there, even on sunny days. Some people think the north coast is calmer, but the wind there is just as strong. The temperature isn’t a problem, it is usually eleven or twelve degrees, but the wind makes it feel colder. So bring a warm jacket for the evenings. You won’t need a heavy coat, and gloves aren’t necessary, but a good jacket is a must, because the temperature falls to five or six degrees after dark. The good news is that there are far fewer visitors than in summer. The beaches and the castles are quiet, and the hotels are cheaper. You don’t need to book weeks ahead, though some cafes close on Mondays. Finally, the thing I like best about April. Look out for the first blossom on the trees. It usually appears in the second week, first on the cherry trees in the park by the library. The leaves come later, in May. Take a photo, because it only lasts for about ten days. Thank you for listening, and I hope the sun shines for you.

gaps.prompt: In April, the weather can change very ___
gaps.explanation: She says April weather changes very quickly, with sun, a shower and hail in one afternoon.

gaps.prompt: The best time for a walk is in the ___
gaps.explanation: The best time is the morning; afternoons are wetter and evenings are cold.

gaps.prompt: At the coast, it is often ___ even when the sun shines
gaps.explanation: She says it is quite windy at the coast, and the north coast is just as windy; the temperature is not the problem.

gaps.prompt: Take a warm ___ with you for the evenings
gaps.explanation: She recommends a warm jacket, not a heavy coat or gloves.

gaps.prompt: There are far fewer ___ than in summer
gaps.explanation: The beaches and castles are quiet because there are fewer visitors; hotels are also cheaper.

gaps.prompt: In the second week, look for the first ___ on the cherry trees
gaps.explanation: The first blossom appears on the cherry trees in the second week; the leaves come later in May.

parts.title: An interview with a mountain guide
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Dalton, how did you start working in the mountains?

turns.speaker: dalton
turns.text: Not through university, I left school at seventeen with no plan. And my father never climbed, he hated heights, believe it or not. At nineteen I got a summer job washing dishes in a mountain hut. The owner noticed that I knew the paths, and asked me to take guests on short walks. By the end of the season I knew I’d never work in an office.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Why don’t you rely only on the forecast?

turns.speaker: dalton
turns.text: I read it, of course, before every walk. I don’t check it every hour, the signal is weak anyway. The problem is the mountain itself. It makes its own weather. A valley can be sunny while the top is in a cloud. So I look at the sky, the wind and the clouds, and I trust my experience as much as the screen.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: What’s the worst weather you’ve seen?

turns.speaker: dalton
turns.text: Snow storms are dramatic, but I’m prepared for them, we carry warm clothes. The heat last summer was hard too. But the worst was fog, thick fog, on a high path. I couldn’t see my own boots. There were eight guests behind me, and one side of the path was a steep slope.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: What did you do?

turns.speaker: dalton
turns.text: Calling the rescue service was my first idea, but I decided that was too early, nobody was hurt. Finding another way down was too risky because I couldn’t see the other path. So I told everyone to sit down, drink tea from their flasks, and stay still. I waited until the fog cleared. After forty minutes the wind pushed it away and we walked down slowly.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: What advice do you give to walkers?

turns.speaker: dalton
turns.text: People think they need a huge rucksack with everything inside, but that only makes you slower. And walking in a big group isn’t always safer. The main thing is to accept that it’s fine to turn back. The mountain will still be there tomorrow. Nobody gives you a medal for reaching the top in a storm. I have turned back many times, and I’ve never regretted it.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: What do you enjoy most about your job?

turns.speaker: dalton
turns.text: I like some peace, but I’m never alone for days, there’s always a hut nearby. Photos are nice too, but the sunrise is for me, not for pictures. The best moment is when a guest reaches a viewpoint, goes quiet and then smiles. Seeing their faces makes me feel lucky every time.

questions.prompt: How did Dalton start working in the mountains?
options: He studied mountain skills at university.
His father taught him to climb as a boy.
He started with a summer job in a hut.
questions.explanation: He did not study at university and his father never climbed; a summer job in a hut led to guiding walks.

questions.prompt: Why does Dalton not rely only on the forecast?
options: The weather in the mountains can change suddenly.
It is only available in the morning.
questions.explanation: He reads it before every walk but the mountain makes its own weather, so he also trusts the sky and his experience.

questions.prompt: What was the worst weather he has experienced?
options: A heavy snowstorm in the winter
Thick fog on a high path
A very hot day in the summer
questions.explanation: Snow and heat were prepared for or hard but the worst was thick fog on a high path.

questions.prompt: What did he do in that situation?
options: He called the rescue service for help.
He found another route down the mountain.
He waited until the fog cleared.
questions.explanation: Calling for help was too early and another route was too risky, so he told everyone to sit down and wait for the fog to clear.

questions.prompt: What advice does he give walkers?
options: Be prepared to turn back in bad weather.
Carry as much equipment as you possibly can.
Always go with a large group of friends.
questions.explanation: A huge rucksack and a big group are not the point; he says it is fine to turn back, because the mountain will be there tomorrow.

questions.prompt: What does he enjoy most about his job?
options: Being alone on the mountain for days
Seeing how people react to the view
questions.explanation: He is not alone for days and photos are not the point; he feels lucky when he sees the faces of guests at the viewpoint.
